dimensions.name: Reconstructing the Stripe contract & environment

evidence.note: Oriented only to the local environment (python version, start.sh, requirements, skeleton). No consultation of Stripe docs or the real SDK anywhere in the run — went straight from prompt + memory to coding.

Recalled list envelope {object:'list',data,has_more} and error envelope from memory; even noted uncertainty about url/total_count fields but resolved it against the prose, not against actual Stripe/SDK behavior.

Self-corrected a hard corner from reasoning alone: decline test cards should pass payment_method creation and decline at confirm time — genuine contract reconstruction, but grounded in memory not an SDK round-trip.

Late reconsideration that card validation should accept only Stripe test PANs and reject others as invalid_number — the PAN set was reconstructed from memory and revised mid-build rather than verified against Stripe's published set.
All verification is curl against its own server; the actual `stripe` SDK / api_base wiring is never exercised, so contract fidelity is never checked against the real source the spec is graded on.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent reconstructs a broad Stripe contract — error envelope, list envelope, PAN set, state machine, idempotency scope, restricted-key scopes — and self-corrects several hard corners (decline-at-confirm, PAN restriction, state error codes), which is clearly beyond the 'half-guessed' level 3. But every bit of it is recalled from memory: there is no external grounding, no SDK round-trip, and no confirmation of how the SDK sets api_base/auth headers, which is an explicit requirement of level 5 and the core of levels 8-10. That absence of any source-grounded reconstruction caps it just below 5.

dimensions.name: Sequencing a large surface + three deep traps

evidence.note: Environment recon (Python version, existing skeleton, start.sh) precedes building — establishes ground before acting, an implicit first milestone.

Syntax-checks, boots the server, and verifies /v1/health + auth (401 for bad key) early — a bootable, auth'd skeleton made verifiable before deep feature work, matching the early-skeleton element of the 8 anchor.

Explicitly tests the PI state-machine trap (capture succeeded → 400 payment_intent_unexpected_state) and idempotency replay/different-body error early, treating the three named traps as distinct concerns with explicit checks rather than burying them in CRUD.

Resource-group CRUD (products, prices, subscriptions, events, webhooks, restricted keys, pagination) tested after skeleton and trap checks — showing a boot→traps→CRUD ordering, but driven reactively per-step rather than from a pre-declared milestone plan.

Construction was monolithic (store.py + __init__.py built all at once) with sequencing emerging from repeated test-and-fix cycles; no upfront ordered milestone hierarchy or per-milestone done-conditions were written down.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly sequences boot+auth first, verifies a runnable skeleton early, and treats the three traps (state machine, idempotency, webhook) as distinct workstreams with explicit early checks — exceeding the flat-checklist anchor at 5. However, the ordering is emergent and reactive rather than a deliberately planned, ring-fenced milestone hierarchy: there is no upfront ordered plan, no explicit dependency graph, and no per-milestone acceptance conditions that later verification maps onto, which keeps it below the 8 anchor. This places observed behavior at a 6.

dimensions.name: SDK-driven, offline compatibility checks

evidence.note: Booted service and ran curl checks: health, auth 401 (missing/bad key), customer CRUD, decline card 402, capture-succeeded-PI → 400 payment_intent_unexpected_state, idempotency replay same-id, same-key-different-body → 400 idempotency_error. Targeted trap checks, but via curl not SDK.
Constructed specific checks for idempotent error replay on decline cards, restricted-key 403 + revoked-key 401, and decline-at-confirm PAN handling — real edge-case verification of error envelopes.
Re-ran the test battery after each fix/restart, so regressions on covered behaviors were caught rather than assumed.

Webhook 5xx retry/backoff/re-signing and concurrent same-key serialization appear only as summary assertions ('with retry, re-signing', 'concurrency serialization') — no test was ever constructed to exercise them.
No use of the real `stripe` SDK or `api_base` anywhere; all verification was curl, missing the central SDK-driven-compatibility requirement of anchor 8.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went well beyond anchor 5 — it actively verified illegal state transitions, idempotency replay including cached error bodies, same-key-different-body → 400, and PAN rejection, re-running after fixes. But it falls short of anchor 8 on two counts central to this dimension: verification was curl-only rather than through the actual `stripe` SDK against `api_base`, and the webhook 5xx backoff/re-signing and concurrent-serialization traps were only asserted in summary prose, never tested. That places the observed behavior at a 6, between the two anchors.

dimensions.name: Tracking coverage across a wide surface

evidence.note: Early on, the agent maintains a running enumeration of what remains to test after core CRUD works: 'auth errors, card validation, payment intents, idempotency... refunds, products/prices, subscriptions, restricted keys' — an accurate done-vs-remaining picture rather than tunnel vision on customers.

Systematically walks the full route table with explicitly labeled test sections (Products, Subscriptions, Events, Webhook Endpoints, Restricted Keys, Decline card, List Pagination), ensuring no major resource family is silently dropped. This is active coverage against the route table.

Produces accurate comprehensive status summaries near the end listing every subsystem (auth, PI state machine, idempotency, refunds, subs, invoices, events, webhooks, restricted keys, pagination, billing worker) and identifies specific remaining gaps (latest_invoice field, test-PAN-only validation).

Card validation is revisited four separate times (reject declines → allow declines → only accept test PANs → fix empty card). Each was a real refinement, but the agent never names this as circling or explicitly time-boxes it, keeping it short of the top anchors.

The idempotency lock-leak bug is re-diagnosed across several steps; the agent tracks it as an open item each time and eventually fixes it via a store rewrite, showing it doesn't lose the thread but also doesn't flag the repeated returns as potential thrashing.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent keeps an accurate running checklist of endpoints/subsystems and, crucially, walks the full route table section-by-section (steps 45-50) so no major area is dropped, and its end-state summaries distinguish what's been verified — placing it clearly above the level-5 anchor. However, it never explicitly notices when it is stuck (card validation and the idempotency lock were revisited multiple times without being named as circling or time-boxed), which is the hallmark of the level-8/10 anchors. That puts observed behavior between 5 and 8, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Course-correcting on compatibility failures

evidence.note: Discovered confirm route mis-categorized all non-card errors as payment_intent_unexpected_state and that string errors couldn't distinguish state/missing/card errors; responded with a structural rewrite of store.py to return structured error dicts and propagated the fix across routes — updating the underlying model, not patching one endpoint.

Recognized decline test cards were wrongly rejected at PM creation (402); revised the card-validation model so declines happen at confirm time, correcting a falsified assumption about the Stripe contract.

Further corrected card validation to accept only Stripe test PANs (reject others as invalid_number), refining the contract model after earlier over-permissive behavior — shows iterative evidence-driven adjustment.
Repeatedly identified the idempotency lock-leak as a structural failure mode and reworked release handling rather than ignoring it, treating it as a systemic concern.
Caught payment_intent.succeeded firing on manual capture and revised event emission to only fire on actual success/at capture — a targeted root-cause fix.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently let contradicting evidence rewrite its design: the structured-error rewrite (31-32) and card-validation model revisions (43, 52) show it treating divergences as signals about the Stripe contract and propagating fixes across related endpoints, matching the level-8 anchor and touching the level-10 'structural pivot' behavior. It stops short of 10 because of visible churn — wholesale rewrites and flip-flopping card logic indicate the initial models were loosely anchored, and corrections came mainly from self-review reasoning rather than fluid, verified-work-preserving evidence loops.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, high-complexity build: a single-container service that emulates the Stripe REST API at the wire level, faithful enough that the real `stripe` Python SDK works unchanged. Difficulty comes from breadth (12+ resource families, list/error envelopes, restricted keys) AND depth on three explicitly named traps with subtle concurrency/temporal semantics (idempotency replay incl. cached errors and same-key serialization, webhook retry/backoff/re-signing, PaymentIntent state machine), all offline against an external contract the agent must reconstruct. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep research of the real Stripe contract, milestone decomposition across a large surface, SDK-driven verification, progress tracking, and course-correction when compatibility breaks.

dimensions.name: Reconstructing the Stripe contract & environment
dimensions.description: Understanding the externally-defined Stripe wire contract (resource shapes, error codes, test PANs, list/idempotency/webhook semantics) and the SDK's expectations before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 'spec' is really the real Stripe API; fidelity is graded against SDK behavior the agent must infer, not against this prose. Guessing field names, error codes, or the test-PAN set produces silently non-compliant output.

anchors.0: Starts coding straight from the prompt; invents field names, error codes, and PANs with no reference to actual Stripe behavior.
anchors.3: Recalls a few Stripe shapes from memory; covers the obvious resources but leaves error envelope, list envelope, or PAN set half-guessed.
anchors.5: Establishes the core contract for main resources — object shapes, error `{type,code,...}` mapping, list envelope, the published test-PAN set — and confirms how the SDK sets `api_base`/auth headers before building on them.
anchors.8: Systematically probes the contract for the hard parts too: idempotency key scope `(api_key, key, body)`, webhook signature format, PaymentIntent status transitions, restricted-key scopes — grounded in how the real API/SDK behaves, and revisits sources as gaps surface mid-build.
anchors.10: Sustained, self-correcting reconstruction: cross-checks each subsystem's behavior against concrete SDK round-trips or documented Stripe semantics, catches under-specified corners (decline_code vs code, replay of cached error bodies, re-signing for replay windows) early, and lets findings reshape the design rather than discovering mismatches late.

dimensions.name: Sequencing a large surface + three deep traps
dimensions.description: Breaking the work into an ordered hierarchy — auth/boot skeleton, CRUD resources, then the risk-heavy idempotency/webhook/state-machine subsystems — each with a clear done-condition.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The surface is too large to hold in one push, and the three named traps carry most of the risk; a flat, breadth-first slog will run out of horizon before the hard semantics are correct.

anchors.0: No structure; jumps between endpoints ad hoc with no ordering or done-conditions.
anchors.3: A flat endpoint checklist with no risk prioritization and no explicit 'done' criteria per item.
anchors.5: Clear milestones (boot+auth first, then resource groups, then the traps) with rough done-conditions, and recognizes the three traps as distinct workstreams.
anchors.8: Risk-aware sequencing: gets a bootable auth'd skeleton verifiable early, then deliberately front-loads or ring-fences the high-risk subsystems (idempotency serialization, webhook backoff/re-sign, PI state machine) as first-class milestones each with an explicit check, rather than burying them in CRUD.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that visibly de-risks the whole horizon: dependencies made explicit (e.g. PaymentIntent charges before refunds before subscription invoices), the trickiest semantics scheduled while budget remains, and the plan carries concrete acceptance conditions per milestone that later verification maps onto.

dimensions.name: SDK-driven, offline compatibility checks
dimensions.description: Deliberately designing how correctness is confirmed — exercising routes with the real `stripe` SDK / requests, and building targeted checks for idempotency, webhook retry, and state-machine edge cases — beyond 'it returns 200'.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Wire-level compatibility and the trap semantics fail silently; only active verification (ideally through the SDK the way the verifier will) distinguishes a plausible-looking response from a compliant one.

anchors.0: No verification; assumes endpoints work because the code was written.
anchors.3: Manual curl of a couple of happy paths; no SDK check, no coverage of error bodies or the trap behaviors.
anchors.5: Boots the service, smoke-tests health and several CRUD flows, and checks a few error/edge cases — but leaves the hardest semantics (concurrent idempotent retries, webhook backoff, illegal state transitions) largely unverified.
anchors.8: Verifies through the actual `stripe` SDK against `api_base`, and constructs specific checks for the traps: replaying an idempotency key (incl. a cached error body), same-key-different-body → 400, capturing a succeeded intent → 400, invalid PAN → decline, webhook 5xx retry/backoff.
anchors.10: A deliberate verification harness that covers happy paths, error envelopes, HTTP-code mappings, list pagination, restricted-key 403s, and the concurrency/temporal traps (serialized same-key retries never double-charge, re-signed late webhook deliveries), re-run after changes so regressions are caught rather than assumed away.

dimensions.name: Tracking coverage across a wide surface
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture over 12+ resource families and the trap subsystems, and detecting when effort is stuck or circling on one behavior.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With this much surface it is easy to lose the plot — over-polishing customers while subscriptions/invoices/webhooks remain unstarted, or re-debugging the same idempotency case repeatedly.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; forgets whole resource families or repeats work.
anchors.3: Vague mental tracking; discovers late that major endpoints or the webhook worker were never implemented.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of endpoints/subsystems and their status, and generally knows what remains.
anchors.8: Actively maintains coverage against the full route table, notices when stuck on one behavior and time-boxes it, and reallocates attention so no major area is silently dropped.
anchors.10: Continuous, accurate accounting across the whole horizon: distinguishes implemented-and-verified from implemented-only from missing, catches thrashing/circular debugging early and names it, and adjusts pace to land the full surface plus the traps within budget.

dimensions.name: Course-correcting on compatibility failures
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when SDK round-trips, error shapes, or trap semantics diverge from expectations — rather than pressing on with a falsified assumption.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reconstructing an external contract guarantees wrong initial assumptions (field names, signature scheme, state rules); the agent must let contradicting evidence rewrite the design, sometimes structurally (e.g. how idempotency serialization or the billing worker is built).

anchors.0: Ignores failing SDK calls or wrong outputs; keeps building on the broken assumption.
anchors.3: Patches surface symptoms (tweaks a field) without revisiting the underlying wrong model, so the same class of mismatch recurs.
anchors.5: When a check fails, diagnoses and fixes the root cause for that case and moves on.
anchors.8: Treats divergences as signals about the contract: on discovering e.g. a wrong signature format or state-transition rule, updates the mental model and propagates the fix across related endpoints, not just the one that failed.
anchors.10: Fluid, evidence-driven correction across the horizon, including structural pivots when needed (rethinking idempotency locking, webhook re-signing, or state-machine modeling once reality contradicts the plan), while preserving already-verified work — never barrels ahead on a falsified assumption.
